verdict.rationale: Romans 11:26 reads 'and in this way all Israel will be saved' (kai houtos pas Israel sothesetai), and three points of pressure in the underlying Greek sit under the proposition. First, the noun 'Israel' (Israel, Strong's G2474, 69 New Testament occurrences) is demonstrably two-valued in Paul himself. Romans 9:6 places 'Israel' (G2474) twice in one clause and explicitly denies that all from 'Israel' (G2474) are 'Israel' (G2474). Galatians 6:16 attaches 'Israel' (G2474) to a benediction on those who walk by the cross-rule ('the Israel of God', ton Israel tou theou). Romans 11:1 to 2 names ethnic Israel as 'his people whom he foreknew' (ton laon autou hon proegno) and emphatically denies that God has rejected them. The same lemma carries ethnic and redefined senses in the same author, so 'all Israel' (pas Israel) in 11:26 is not univocal (does not have a single fixed meaning). Second, the adverb 'in this way' (houtos, Strong's G3779, 215 New Testament occurrences) is lexically a manner adverb ('in this way'); the temporal-sequential sense ('and then') cannot be extracted from morphology (the word form) and depends on the preceding 'until' clause (achri-clause) to license it. Third, the adjective 'irrevocable' (ametameletos, Strong's G0278) occurs only twice in the canon (Romans 11:29; 2 Corinthians 7:10), which forces the irrevocability claim to lean on a near-hapax (a word that occurs only once or nearly once in the entire Bible). The future passive 'will be saved' (sothesetai, from Strong's G4982) plus the unconditional Abrahamic 'everlasting covenant' (berit olam, Genesis 17:7 to 8) plus the new covenant named to 'the house of Israel' (bet Yisrael, Jeremiah 31:31 to 37) plus the future mourning of Jerusalem over the pierced one (Zechariah 12:10) together establish a durable covenant standing and a coming corporate turning, but the lexemes (vocabulary items) do not by themselves rank an ethnic-corporate-event reading against a redefined-people-of-God reading. The pattern is materially contested, so the proposition is disputed.

scripture.force: The crux clause 'and in this way all Israel will be saved' (kai houtos pas Israel sothesetai) compounds three contested lexical points. The verb 'will be saved' (sothesetai) is future passive of 'to save' (sozo, Strong's G4982), so an eschatological (end-time) deliverance is asserted, but the verb alone does not fix who its subject is or whether it names a single visible event. The quantifier 'all' (pas, Strong's G3956) with 'Israel' (Israel, G2474) fixes scope only relative to whatever 'Israel' denotes. The adverb 'in this way' (houtos, Strong's G3779, 215 New Testament occurrences) is a manner adverb in its core lexical sense ('in this way, after this manner'); a strictly temporal-sequential reading ('and then') is not a morphological feature (a feature of the word form) of the word and is inferred only by reading 'in this way' (houtos) as picking up the 'until' clause (achri-clause) of verse 25. The cited oracle (Isaiah 59:20 to 21 plus Isaiah 27:9) supplies the Deliverer who comes 'from Zion' (ek Sion) and 'will turn away ungodliness' (apostrepsei asebeias), grounding the saving act in a redemptive intervention. The lexical bundle anchors a coming deliverance but does not by morphology (word form) rank the ethnic-corporate reading against a redefined or remnant reading.

The partial hardening ('hardening in part', apo merous porosis) of Israel holds 'until' (achri hou, Strong's G0891 plus the relative pronoun, 'until') 'the fulness of the Gentiles comes in' (pleroma ton ethnon eiselthe). The preposition 'until' (achri) is consistently a terminus marker (a marker of an end-point) across its 50 New Testament occurrences, setting a boundary point for the hardening. What 'until' (achri) does NOT specify by morphology (word form) is what happens after the terminus (end-point), whether a single national event, an ongoing ingathering, or simply the end of the hardening as such. The terminus reading is genuinely there in the word, but the inference to a future visible salvation of the nation as a whole is supplied by reading 'in this way' (houtos) in verse 26 sequentially rather than modally (as a manner expression).

Paul opens the unit with 'has God rejected his people? By no means!' (me apesato ho theos ton laon autou? me genoito), denying with the strongest available negation that God has rejected his people, and grounds the denial in his own descent as 'an Israelite' (Israelites, Strong's G2475) from the seed of Abraham. The pairing of 'his people' (laos autou) with the foreknowledge verb in verse 2 ('whom he foreknew', hon proegno) gives ethnic Israel a divinely held standing and is the load-bearing premise for any future-for-Israel reading. It does not itself assert a future mass salvation, so it supplies the covenant premise but not the disputed conclusion.

Israel is 'enemies' (echthroi) with respect to the gospel but 'beloved' (agapetoi) with respect to election, 'on account of the fathers' (dia tous pateras). The patriarchal grounding ties present standing to the Abrahamic promise. Verse 29 then declares 'for irrevocable are the gifts and the calling of God' (ametameleta gar ta charismata kai he klesis tou theou), that the gifts and calling are 'not to be repented of, irrevocable.' The word 'irrevocable' (ametameletos, Strong's G0278) occurs only twice in the canon (here and 2 Corinthians 7:10, where it modifies a repentance 'not to be regretted'), so the irrevocability claim leans on a near-hapax (a word that occurs only once or nearly once in the entire Bible) whose semantic field is 'never recalled, never withdrawn.' The word strongly supports an unbroken covenant standing for ethnic Israel, but the leap from 'gifts and calling are irrevocable' to 'a future visible corporate salvation event' remains an interpretive step beyond the lexeme (vocabulary item).

God 'establishes' (hekim, Strong's H6965) his 'covenant' (berit, Strong's H1285) between himself and Abraham and 'his seed after him' (zaro acharav) 'throughout their generations' (le-dorotam) 'for an everlasting covenant' (li-berit olam), 'to be God to you' (li-hyot lekha le-Elohim). The pairing 'everlasting covenant' (berit olam) marks the covenant as perpetual, and verse 8 extends it to the land as 'an everlasting possession' (ahuzzat olam). The lexical force grounds an enduring relationship with the seed of Abraham. It is the Old Testament root of the irrevocability claim Paul echoes with 'irrevocable' (ametameleta), but the covenant text speaks of relationship and land, not explicitly of a future mass conversion.

The new 'covenant' (berit) is cut with 'the house of Israel' (bet Yisrael) (and verse 31 with 'the house of Judah', bet Yehudah), with the torah (law/instruction) written 'on their heart' (al libbam) and the covenant formula 'I will be their God and they shall be my people.' The naming of the house of Israel and house of Judah as the covenant partners keeps an ethnic-national referent in view, and verses 35 to 37 stake the continuance of 'the seed of Israel' (zera Yisrael) as 'a nation before me' (goy lefanai) on the 'fixed order' (choq) of sun, moon and sea ('sun, moon, stars', sham shemesh, yareah, kokhavim) and the immeasurability of the heavens. The lexical pattern guarantees Israel's permanence as a people but describes covenant renewal and forgiveness, not a single future visible salvation event.

YHWH 'pours out' (shafakhti, Strong's H8210) 'a spirit of grace and supplications' (ruah hen ve-tahanunim) on the house of David and the inhabitants of Jerusalem, and they 'look on' (ve-hibitu, Strong's H5027) 'the one whom they pierced' (eth asher daqaru, Strong's H1856, 'whom they pierced') and 'mourn' (ve-safdu, Strong's H5594), with the verb 'to be bitter' (marar, Strong's H4843) describing bitter lamentation 'as one mourns for an only child' (ke-misped al ha-yahid), 'and bitter as one is bitter over a firstborn' (ve-hamer ke-hamer al ha-bekhor). The text portrays a future corporate turning of the people of Jerusalem toward the pierced one. Whether this is a single visible salvation of the ethnic people as a whole, or a representative corporate turning fulfilled in part at Pentecost (Acts 2) and extended in the gospel age, is not settled by the lexemes (vocabulary items) alone.

Two chapters before Romans 11:26 Paul writes 'for not all those from Israel are Israel' (ou gar pantes hoi ex Israel houtoi Israel). 'Israel' (Strong's G2474) appears twice in one clause with two distinct referents: a wider ethnic descent ('out from Israel') and a narrower theological remnant ('these are Israel'). Verses 7 to 8 reinforce this by distinguishing 'the children of the flesh' (ta tekna tes sarkos) from 'the children of the promise' (ta tekna tes epangelias) and reckoning only the latter 'as seed' (eis sperma). This intra-Pauline polysemy (multiple meanings within the same author) of 'Israel' within three chapters of 11:26 is the principal lexical reason 'all Israel' (pas Israel) in 11:26 cannot be assumed to denote the ethnic nation as a whole; the same author has just demonstrated that the noun does not require that referent.

Paul closes with peace and mercy 'and upon the Israel of God' (kai epi ton Israel tou theou). The conjunction 'and' (kai) is ambiguous between additive ('and also upon') and explicative (clarifying, 'that is, upon'), and the referent of 'Israel' (Strong's G2474) here is contested between believing ethnic Jews and the believing community as a whole. The lexeme (vocabulary item) 'Israel' (G2474) itself does the same double duty here that it does at Romans 9:6, supplying a New Testament data point for a redefined or extended use of the name. This complicates a reading of Romans 11:26 that assumes 'Israel' (G2474) must denote the ethnic nation.

'And if you are Christ's, then you are Abraham's seed, heirs according to promise' (ei de hymeis Christou, ara tou Abraam sperma este, kat' epangelian kleronomoi). The lexemes (vocabulary items) 'Abraham's seed' (sperma Abraam, Strong's G4690 plus G0011) and 'heirs' (kleronomoi, Strong's G2818) are applied to all who are 'in Christ' (en Christo), irrespective of ethnicity, redistributing covenant-heir vocabulary to a non-ethnic body. Combined with verse 7 ('those of faith, these are sons of Abraham', hoi ek pisteos houtoi huioi eisin Abraam), this supports a reading in which Abrahamic-covenant categories are inherited through faith. It complicates any reading that strictly limits the Abrahamic-promise vocabulary to ethnic descent.

Gentiles before Christ were 'alienated from the commonwealth of Israel' (apellotriomenoi tes politeias tou Israel) and 'strangers to the covenants of promise' (xenoi ton diathekon tes epangelias). Here 'Israel' (Strong's G2474) names the historic covenant people from which Gentiles were excluded; verses 13 to 16 then say that Christ has 'made the two one' (ta amphotera hen) and broken down 'the dividing wall of the fence' (mesotoichon tou fragmou, Strong's G3320 plus G5418) to create 'one new man' (hena kainon anthropon). The lexical pattern uses 'Israel' (G2474) in a clearly ethnic-historic sense, then describes Gentile incorporation into the same covenant body, supplying both a non-redefined use of 'Israel' and a one-new-man motif at once.

Believers are addressed as 'a chosen race' (genos eklekton, Strong's G1085 plus G1588), 'a royal priesthood' (basileion hierateuma, Strong's G0934 plus G2406), 'a holy nation' (ethnos hagion, Strong's G1484 plus G0040), and 'a people for his possession' (laos eis peripoiesin, Strong's G2992), reusing the Exodus 19:5 to 6 and Isaiah 43 vocabulary that originally named ethnic Israel. The lexeme (vocabulary item) 'Israel' (G2474) itself is not present here, so this is a transfer of covenant-people titles rather than a renaming of the addressees as 'Israel.' The lexical pattern supports a redistribution of Israel's titular vocabulary to the believing community but does not by itself absorb the noun 'Israel' (G2474) into the church.

The disciples ask 'are you at this time restoring the kingdom to Israel?' (ei en to chrono touto apokathistaneis ten basileian to Israel?). The verb 'to restore' (apokathistemi, Strong's G0600) means 'restore to a prior state.' Jesus' answer in verse 7 ('it is not for you to know times or seasons', ouk hymon estin gnonai chronous e kairous) corrects the timing but does not deny the category of restoration or the propriety of using 'Israel' (G2474) in this sense. Lexically the exchange leaves the restoration-to-Israel hope intact and denies only the knowability of its timing. This supports a future-for-Israel reading without specifying scope or whether the restoration is realized within the gospel-age incorporation of the nations or as a distinct future event.

complicating_texts.resolution: Paul's own statement 'for not all those from Israel are Israel' (ou gar pantes hoi ex Israel houtoi Israel) establishes that 'Israel' (Strong's G2474) carries a narrower-than-ethnic sense within the same argument. This means 'all Israel' (pas Israel) in 11:26 cannot be read as unambiguously denoting the entire ethnic people; the same lemma in the same author refuses that constraint. The proposition is graded disputed rather than affirmed because of this intra-Pauline polysemy (multiple meanings within the same author).

The phrase 'the Israel of God' (ton Israel tou theou) places 'Israel' (G2474) in apposition (a noun placed beside another to identify it) or addition to those who 'walk by this rule' ('rule', toi kanoni). The conjunction 'and' (kai) can be additive (a separate group of believing ethnic Jews) or explicative (clarifying, 'that is, the Israel of God'), and the lexeme (vocabulary item) 'Israel' (G2474) itself permits both. Direct lexical query confirms 'Israel' (G2474) is used at Galatians 6:16, Ephesians 2:12 (commonwealth of Israel in an ethnic-historic sense), Romans 9:6 (two referents in one clause), and Romans 11:1 to 2 (ethnic Israel as 'his people', ton laon autou). The noun is genuinely two-valued in the Pauline corpus, and this Galatians datum is the strongest single complicating reference for the ethnic-corporate reading of Romans 11:26.

The terminus (end-point) 'until' (achri hou, 'until') in verse 25 sets an end to the hardening but does not by morphology (word form) determine what follows the terminus (end-point). The adverb 'in this way' (houtos) in verse 26 (Strong's G3779) is a manner adverb lexically ('in this way'); a strictly temporal-then-national reading is not encoded in the word and must be inferred from the 'until' clause (achri-clause) it follows. Both modal (manner-based, 'and in this manner') and sequential-modal (combining order and manner, 'and then, in this way') are lexically licensed. The proposition leans on the sequential-modal reading, which is defensible but not lexically forced.

'Those of faith, these are sons of Abraham' (hoi ek pisteos houtoi huioi eisin Abraam) applies covenant-descent vocabulary ('sons of Abraham', huioi Abraam) to believers irrespective of ethnicity. Together with Galatians 3:29 (heirs 'according to promise', kat' epangelian), this complicates any reading that confines Abrahamic-promise vocabulary to ethnic descent and therefore complicates the inference from the Abrahamic 'everlasting covenant' (berit olam) directly to a future event for the ethnic nation as a corporate body.

The Exodus and Isaiah titles ('chosen race', genos eklekton; 'royal priesthood', basileion hierateuma; 'holy nation', ethnos hagion; 'people', laos) are transferred to believers, but the noun 'Israel' (G2474) itself is not used of the church here. The lexical pattern supports a transfer of covenant-people titles to the believing community without absorbing the noun 'Israel' into the church. This complicates a strong supersessionist reading (the view that the church replaces Israel) that would identify the church as Israel and equally complicates a strong ethnic-only reading that would deny any transfer of Israel's vocabulary to believers.

variants.note: The bundle reports 'not_in_ecm_scope' true and supplies no variant units (places where manuscripts differ) for the Romans 11 anchor verses. The apparatus markers (notes in the critical edition of New Testament textual variants) in Romans 11:25 (the letter 'eta') and 11:26 ('the one who delivers', rhuomenos) are orthographic (spelling) and citation-form variants that do not bear on the disputed referent of 'all Israel' (pas Israel) or on the future passive 'will be saved' (sothesetai). Zechariah 12:10 has a known textual question between 'they pierced' (daqaru) and the Septuagint (the Greek Old Testament) rendering, but it does not affect the lexical force of the corporate mourning. The verdict holds across the plausible readings.

competing_lens_verdicts.rationale: Reads 'all Israel' (pas Israel) as the ethnic nation viewed corporately, takes 'in this way' (houtos) as sequential-modal (combining order and manner) after the 'until' terminus (end-point, achri-terminus) of the Gentile fulness, and reads the 'irrevocable' (ametameleta) of Romans 11:29 plus the 'everlasting covenant' (berit olam) of Genesis 17:7 to 8 plus the corporate mourning of Zechariah 12:10 over the pierced one as converging on a future visible salvation of the people. The strongest lexical anchors for this reading are the near-hapax (a word that occurs only once or nearly once in the entire Bible) 'irrevocable' (ametameletos) guaranteeing the gifts and calling cannot be withdrawn, the 'until' terminus (achri-terminus) marking an end to the hardening, and the disciples' 'restoration' question (apokathistemi-question) in Acts 1:6 that Jesus does not lexically deny but only relocates in time.

Reads 'all Israel' (pas Israel) as either the elect remnant of ethnic Israel summed across history or the combined Jew and Gentile people of God in Christ, takes 'in this way' (houtos) as modal (manner-based, 'in this way, by the gospel'), and grounds the redefinition in Romans 9:6 ('Israel', G2474, as two-valued in Paul himself), Galatians 6:16 ('the Israel of God', ton Israel tou theou), Galatians 3:7 and 29 ('those of faith', hoi ek pisteos, are sons and heirs of Abraham), Ephesians 2:11 to 22 (the wall is broken down, the two are made 'one new man', hena kainon anthropon), and the redistribution of Israel's titles to believers in 1 Peter 2:9 ('chosen race', genos eklekton; 'royal priesthood', basileion hierateuma; 'holy nation', ethnos hagion). On this reading the salvation of 'all Israel' (pas Israel) is the in-Christ ingathering itself, not a separate future event.

Affirms an unbroken covenant standing for ethnic Israel from Romans 11:1 to 2 and 11:28 to 29 plus a future large-scale conversion of ethnic Jews at the close of the gospel age, while denying a distinct national-territorial program separate from the one people of God in Christ. The lexemes (vocabulary items) 'irrevocable' (ametameleta, Strong's G0278), 'his people whom he foreknew' (laos autou hon proegno, Romans 11:2), and corporate mourning at Zechariah 12:10 support the future-conversion side, while the polysemy (multiple meanings) of 'Israel' (G2474) in Paul and the one-new-man vocabulary of Ephesians 2 constrain it. The morphology (word form) supports this mediating reading at least as well as the strict ethnic-corporate-event reading.

hermeneutics.notes: The verdict turns on three lexical facts the morphology (word form) does not adjudicate (does not settle): the referent of 'Israel' (Strong's G2474) in Romans 11:26 given its proven polysemy (multiple meanings) at Romans 9:6 and Galatians 6:16, the force of 'in this way' (houtos, Strong's G3779) (modal, manner-based, versus sequential-modal, combining order and manner), and the scope of 'all' (pas, Strong's G3956) with 'Israel' (G2474). Each lens above can be assembled from real lexical data. The proposition is disputed because the words supply all three lenses and rank none.

stem_audit.neutralized_form: Romans 11:26 states that 'and in this way all Israel will be saved' (kai houtos pas Israel sothesetai); the lexical question is what 'all Israel' (pas Israel) denotes (ethnic nation as a corporate future body, elect ethnic remnant across history, or combined Jew and Gentile people of God in Christ) and whether 'and in this way' (kai houtos) is modal (manner-based) or sequential, which together control whether a future visible salvation of the ethnic nation as such is asserted.
stem_audit.notes: The original stem encodes a specific reading ('future, visible salvation of ethnic Israel as a people') of contested lexemes (vocabulary items). 'As a people' presupposes the ethnic-corporate referent of 'all Israel' (pas Israel) that Romans 9:6 and Galatians 6:16 show is not the only available sense, and 'future, visible' presupposes a sequential-modal (combining order and manner) reading of 'in this way' (houtos). The verdict is derived on the original stem and graded disputed because the neutral form exposes multiple defensible lexical readings the morphology (word form) does not rank.

lay_summary: The proposition stands on Romans 11:26, where Paul writes 'and in this way all Israel will be saved' (kai houtos pas Israel sothesetai). Three small pieces of Greek do the heavy lifting, and each is genuinely open. First, the noun 'Israel' (Israel, Strong's G2474) is two-valued in Paul himself. Only two chapters earlier, in Romans 9:6, he writes that 'not all those from Israel are Israel,' using the same word twice in one sentence with two different meanings. In Galatians 6:16 he speaks of 'the Israel of God' (ton Israel tou theou), attached to those who walk by his cross-rule, and the word 'Israel' there is contested between believing ethnic Jews and the believing community as a whole. So 'all Israel' (pas Israel) in Romans 11:26 could mean the ethnic nation viewed as a body, or the saved remnant of that nation gathered across all of history, or Jewish and Gentile believers together. The word itself does not pick. Second, the little adverb 'in this way' (houtos), translated 'so' or 'in this way' or 'and then,' is by default a manner word, not a time word. A strict 'and then, after the Gentiles' reading is a context-driven inference, not a feature of the word itself. Third, the rare word translated 'irrevocable' (ametameletos) in verse 29 appears only twice in the whole New Testament, here and in 2 Corinthians 7:10. That word does guarantee that God's gifts and calling for ethnic Israel cannot be withdrawn, which is the strongest single anchor on the future-for-Israel side. The surrounding context strengthens that side further. Paul says God has not rejected his foreknown people in Romans 11:1 to 2. The Old Testament backs him up. Genesis 17 makes the covenant ('berit') with Abraham and his seed an everlasting covenant ('berit olam'), Jeremiah 31 names the house of Israel and Judah as the covenant partners and ties their survival as a nation to the unbreakable order of sun, moon, and sea, and Zechariah 12:10 pictures the people of Jerusalem mourning bitterly (the verb 'marar' meaning to be bitter) as they look on the one they pierced. The other side has lexical weight too. Galatians 3 calls those who believe sons of Abraham and heirs of the promise, Ephesians 2 says the wall between Jew and Gentile is broken down to make 'one new man' (hena kainon anthropon), and 1 Peter 2:9 transfers Israel's titles, 'chosen race' (genos eklekton), 'royal priesthood' (basileion hierateuma), 'holy nation' (ethnos hagion), to believers. Acts 1:6 to 7 keeps a 'restore the kingdom to Israel' (apokathistemi, to restore) hope intact but refuses to set its time. Both lenses are built from real words. The Greek and Hebrew together supply both a durable standing for ethnic Israel and a redefinition vocabulary in Christ, and they do not rank the two. That is why the lexical pattern here is contested rather than settled in either direction.
